To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) concentrations of TCDD, TCDD and selected metals remained at pre-operatinal levels during the first 5 years of operation of an MSW combustor and landfill; 2) mercury and selenium were found at their lowest concentrations during the fifth year; 3) lead concentrations in ibis nestings were higher during Years 1 and 5 compared to Year 0; and 4) the MSW combustor cannot be ruled out as the source of lead in ib

TCDD and TCDF were not detected in anhinga and ibis eggs and nestlings during the first five (5) years of MSW combustor operation, and that the concentrations of most metals were similar to those measured in anhingas and white ibises collected from a colony near a MSW landfill in 1992, prior to MSW combustor construction.
TCDD, TCDD and selected metal concentrations measured in anhinga and ibis eggs and nestlings collected from a colony near a MSW combustor and ash dump did not increase significantly over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of avian biomonitoring to detect changes in the environment resulting from the operation of a municipal solid-wastes combustor.
the effects of the MSW combustor on anhingas and white ibises.
evaluating whether the MSW combustor has affected the concentrations of environmental contaminants in eggs and nestling birds of the anhinga and ibis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MSW combustor and ash disposal site have not caused significant environmental impacts to anhinga and white ibis populations in the vicinity of the facility during the five years of operation.
there were no detectable effects from the MSW combustor on the concentrations of TCDD, TCDD, and selected metals in anhingas and white ibises.
the MSW combustor and ash land fill did not appear to pose any threat to anhinga and ibis reproductive success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MSW combustor did not appear to have had a significant impact on the contaminant residues in anhingas and white ibises during the first five year of facility operation.
the MSW combustor did not cause significant changes in the levels of TCDD, TCDD, or metals in anhinga and white ibis eggs and nestlings.
there was little evidence of increased exposure to environmental contaminants in these birds during the first five year of facility operation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biomonitoring of environmental contaminants can be used as a tool to determine whether a source of contamination is operating as designed.
the MSW combustor did not appear to be a source of significant environmental contamination for the birds in this study.
, although the MSW combustor and ash disposal area are adjacent to the colony, the concentrations of contaminants measured in the eggs and nestlings did not increase over time.
